parts: Rutherford fired α-particles at a thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, a few were deflected through large angles, and about 1 in 8000 bounced back.

Conclusions (the nuclear model): (1) most of the atom is empty space; (2) all the positive charge and almost all the mass are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus (about 10⁻¹⁵ m, against an atom of about 10⁻¹⁰ m); (3) electrons revolve round the nucleus, with the electrostatic attraction providing the centripetal force.
The distance of closest approach of an α-particle scattered back through 180° gives an upper estimate of the nuclear radius.
Drawbacks: by classical theory a revolving electron should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus, so atoms would be unstable and give continuous spectra.
Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom

Postulates: (1) electrons move only in certain stationary orbits without radiating; (2) in these orbits the angular momentum mvr = nh/2π (h/2π in the ground state); (3) radiation is emitted or absorbed only when the electron jumps between orbits: hν = E₂ − E₁.

Results: the orbit radius rₙ = n²a₀, with a₀ = 0.53 Å, so the third orbit is 9a₀ and r₂ : r₁ = 4 : 1. The energy Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV, giving −13.6, −3.4 and −1.51 eV for n = 1, 2, 3. The ratio of the first and second excited states is E₂ : E₃ = 9 : 4.
The ionization energy of hydrogen is 13.6 eV; for hydrogen-like He⁺ it is 13.6Z² = 54.4 eV.
Lyman series: n₁ = 1, ultraviolet. Balmer: n₁ = 2, visible (e.g. 4861 Å, 6563 Å). Paschen: n₁ = 3, infrared. Brackett: n₁ = 4. Pfund: n₁ = 5, far infrared.
The shortest wavelength comes from the largest energy jump (e.g. 6 → 1). The longest Paschen line (4 → 3) is λ = 144/7R. The transition 3 → 1 gives 1/λ = 8R/9, i.e. λ ≈ 102.6 nm (Lyman).
From level n the maximum number of spectral lines is n(n − 1)/2; for n = 4 it is 6.
The maximum number of electrons in the outermost shell of any atom is 8.
